title: Loyalty Matching Company's Loyalty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need employees who are loyal to the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I promise to be as loyal to the company as the company is to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good enough?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop being a jerk.

situation: The Boss declares in a meeting that he needs employees who are loyal to the company. Dilbert replies that he will be exactly as loyal to the company as the company is to him, then asks if that is good enough. Alice, sitting nearby, tells him to stop being a jerk.
punchline: Dilbert's promise of reciprocal loyalty implies the company shows its employees very little loyalty, so his pledge is effectively a promise of none.
summary: An employee answers a demand for corporate loyalty by offering to return exactly the amount he receives, which is a pointed insult disguised as agreement.

title: Work Less Fun Than TikTok

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm hearing you are addicted to TikTok videos and are not getting your work done.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It isn't my fault that you can't make my job more fun than the alternatives.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you know why we pay you?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I assumed you were just being polite.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, confronts an employee who is looking at his phone and has reportedly been watching TikTok videos instead of working. The employee blames management for not making the job more entertaining than the alternatives. When the Boss asks why the company pays him, the employee answers that he assumed it was just politeness.
punchline: The employee sarcastically implies that his salary is a courtesy rather than payment for work, turning the Boss's reprimand back on him.
summary: A manager scolds a phone-obsessed worker, who replies that dull work is the manager's fault and treats his paycheck as a mere kindness.

title: Marketing Versus Engineering: Oreo Crumbs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever imagine what it would be like to work in marketing instead of engineering?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I always assumed it would feel like eating ice cream while wearing silk pajamas on a warm summer day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What does your current job feel like?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sleeping naked on Oreo crumbs.

situation: Dilbert asks a fellow engineer at the coffee maker whether he ever imagines working in marketing instead of engineering. The coworker describes marketing as a blissful, luxurious existence. When asked what his current job feels like, he gives a deliberately uncomfortable comparison.
punchline: The coworker's idealized view of marketing is set against his own engineering job, which he likens to the miserable, itchy discomfort of sleeping naked on Oreo crumbs.
summary: Over coffee, an engineer pictures marketing as pure luxury while describing his own job as a gritty, irritating ordeal.

title: Bob Debates by Accusing Fear

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Bob.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bob likes to debate, but he isn't good at it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When you disagree with Bob, he will insist that the only reason you disagree is that you are afraid.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you get vaccinated, Bob will say you are afraid of catching a sniffle.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you don't get vaccinated, Bob will say you are afraid of getting the shot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bob believes your thinking process does not extend beyond your fears.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's because Bob is a moron who projects his one-dimensional worldview on others.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Sounds like you're afraid to admit I'm a better debater than you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There it is.

situation: Dogbert introduces a colleague named Bob to a meeting and explains his debating style. Bob dismisses every disagreement as fear, whether people get vaccinated or not. After Dogbert calls him a moron who projects his worldview on others, Bob responds by claiming Dogbert is afraid to admit Bob is the better debater.
punchline: Bob proves Dogbert's description right by immediately accusing him of being afraid, using the very fallacy Dogbert just described.
summary: A pooch lays out how a coworker argues by claiming opponents are scared, and the coworker obligingly demonstrates the habit on the spot.

title: Wisdom Is Just Nice-Sounding Words

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your video on lassoing the energy of the cosmos using ropes of love is going viral.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't understand why anyone thinks your gobbledygook is wisdom when it is so obviously nothing but words that sound good in sentences.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's all wisdom is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to think that isn't true.

situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert, who is sitting on the couch, that his video about lassoing cosmic energy with ropes of love has gone viral. Dilbert, looking at his phone, complains that it is obvious nonsense that merely sounds good. Dogbert calmly replies that this is all wisdom really is, and Dilbert says he needs to believe otherwise.
punchline: Dogbert suggests that wisdom is nothing more than pleasant-sounding words, and Dilbert cannot bear the cynical implication that he has just been shown to be right about his own gibberish critique.
summary: A viral video of New Age babble leads Dilbert to scoff at its popularity until Dogbert suggests that profundity is mostly good-sounding phrasing.

title: Circle Back Never Comes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have the approved vendor list?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let me circle back to you on that.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Much, much later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I never heard from him again.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why do I have a beard?

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker in procurement for the approved vendor list. The coworker promises to circle back, and in the final panel, much, much later, Dilbert is old and bearded with a cane, having never heard back. Dogbert has grown a beard too and wonders why.
punchline: The coworker's promise to 'circle back' was an empty brush-off, and so much time passes waiting for a reply that Dilbert and Dogbert grow old and sprout beards.
summary: A routine request gets a vague stalling promise, and the wait stretches on so long that the requester ages visibly.

title: Dave's Meaningless Buzzword Update

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: Dave, do you have an update to share?

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Yes, I can speak to that.

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: At the end of the day, it is what it is.

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: Are you done?

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Strategy, structure and people!

situation: At a meeting, a colleague with a two-tufted hairstyle asks Dave for a status update. Dave responds with empty clichés like 'it is what it is,' prompting the leader to ask if he's finished, and Dave simply throws his arms up and shouts 'Strategy, structure and people!' Dilbert watches from the side of the table.
punchline: Dave's 'update' contains no actual information, just corporate buzzwords strung together to sound meaningful and busy.
summary: A man asked for a project update fills the time with vague platitudes and a triumphant buzzword finale without saying anything of substance.
keywords: at the end of the day

title: Wally's Pronoun Checkmate Backfires

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Alex, and my pronouns are she, her, and they.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm Wally, and I identify as a guy who doesn't use the right pronouns.

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Check-mate.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're a graceful loser.

situation: A new coworker named Alex introduces themselves by listing their pronouns. Wally, seated with his coffee, responds by claiming an identity as someone who doesn't use the right pronouns. Alex declares checkmate, and Wally concedes by calling Alex a graceful loser, even though Wally is the one who was just beaten.
punchline: Wally tries to turn pronoun introductions into a clever gotcha, but Alex's 'checkmate' shows Wally's stunt was easily outmaneuvered, and Wally's 'graceful loser' line is him awkwardly admitting defeat while pretending he won.
summary: A coworker's pronoun introduction gets mocked by Wally's sarcastic self-identification, but the exchange ends with Wally conceding the round.

title: Teamwork Makes the Cream Twerk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And always remember, teamwork makes the... cream twerk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In hindsight, I shouldn't have started the sentence if I didn't know how to end it.

setting: Office meeting room and break area
situation: The Boss addresses his employees with a motivational teamwork slogan but garbles the ending into nonsense. The employees (Dilbert, Wally and Alice) stand there with question marks over their heads, confused. Afterward, the Boss admits to Catbert that he shouldn't have begun the sentence without knowing how to finish it.
punchline: The Boss botches a motivational teamwork slogan by blurting out a nonsense phrase, then offers an obvious bit of self-aware hindsight about starting a sentence he couldn't finish.
summary: A manager's attempt at an inspiring teamwork saying collapses into gibberish, leaving his staff baffled and him reflecting on his own improvisation.

title: Dogbert Secretly Owns TikTok

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't know if I mentioned I built a user interface to control the world.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I had to hide my ownership of it so no large military power would know what I was up to.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you call this user interface?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: TikTok. Have you heard of it?

setting: Office desk with coffee mugs and a phone
situation: Dogbert casually tells Dilbert he has built a user interface for controlling the world and concealed his ownership so no military power would catch on. When Dilbert asks what it is called, Dogbert holds up a phone and reveals it is TikTok.
punchline: Dogbert claims to secretly own TikTok, satirizing fears that the app is a tool for world domination and influence, while the popular app's ubiquity makes the supposedly hidden plan absurdly obvious.
summary: Dogbert confesses to Dilbert that his hidden world-controlling interface is actually the wildly popular social media app on his phone.

title: Workplace Culture Means Hoping for Death

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do I need to come to the office to use the laptop I bring home every night?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to come here to get the workplace culture.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I do here is work in my cubicle and hope for death.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's our culture.

setting: Office, at a conference or desk area
situation: Dilbert asks his boss why he must commute to the office when he already takes his laptop home every night. The boss claims the office is needed to absorb the workplace culture. Dilbert replies that all he does there is work in a cubicle and hope for death, and the boss agrees that this is the culture.
punchline: The boss unwittingly confirms that the company's culture is misery and despair, undermining his own justification for mandatory office attendance.
summary: A reluctant employee challenges a return-to-office rule and gets his grim daily routine confirmed as the very culture he is being asked to commute for.

title: Dogbert Controls Minds Through TikTok

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: With my user interface for controlling human minds, I can create mass hysteria with one button.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Say goodbye to eggs.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does anyone else know you own TikTok?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm counting on no one believing it.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dogbert perched on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch holding a phone and boasts that his mind-control interface can cause mass hysteria with a single button. He presses it to make people give up eggs, then Dilbert asks whether anyone knows Dogbert owns TikTok. Dogbert replies that he is counting on nobody believing it.
punchline: Dogbert's secret ownership of TikTok stays safe because the idea that one dog could manipulate millions through a social media app sounds too absurd to be believed, which is also a jab at how social media can sway the public.
summary: A scheming dog secretly owns a wildly popular app and uses it to sway the masses, trusting that nobody would credit such a claim.

title: Dogbert's Unethical Instagram Guru Scheme

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's it going with your unethical scheme to become an internet success guru?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not bad. I gained twelve million followers on Instagram in one week.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How's honesty working out for you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up.

situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert, who is working at a laptop, how his unethical plan to become an internet success guru is going. Dogbert reports that he gained twelve million Instagram followers in a week, then turns the question around and asks Dilbert how honesty is working out for him. Dilbert has no good reply.
punchline: Dogbert's dishonest scheme is wildly successful, so he mocks Dilbert's integrity, implying that honesty gets you nowhere compared to shameless self-promotion.
summary: A thriving con artist dog rubs his rapid social media fame in the face of his scrupulous, struggling friend.

title: Is This Guru Brilliant or Dumb?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Have you seen the viral video of the guru who knows everything about the universe?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: ...Energy creates motion, and motion activates the mind, and the mind creates meaning, and the meaning is energy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that brilliant or dumb? I can't tell.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I was hoping you could tell me.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether he has seen a viral video of a guru who supposedly knows everything about the universe, then holds up his phone and recites the guru's circular statement about energy, motion, mind and meaning. Dilbert admits he cannot tell if it is profound or nonsense, and the Boss reveals he was hoping Dilbert could judge it for him.
punchline: The Boss is so unable to evaluate the guru's circular pseudo-wisdom himself that he relies on Dilbert to tell him whether it is brilliant or dumb, showing how hard it is to tell profound-sounding gibberish from real insight.
summary: A manager shares a viral guru clip whose cyclical babble sounds deep but means nothing, and cannot decide for himself whether it is genius or nonsense.

title: Slide Deck Busywork Feels Like Crime

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I move these objects around on my slide deck, it will feel as if I am working.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Working, working, working.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The difference between working on a slide deck and committing a white-collar crime is narrowing.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, then a home-like room with a couch
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer rearranging objects on a slide deck, thinking that it will make him feel productive. He keeps typing and thinking 'working' over and over. In the last panel he stands next to Dogbert on a couch and remarks that slide deck work is starting to resemble white-collar crime.
punchline: Dilbert realizes that shuffling slide objects to look busy is essentially fraudulent, like faking productivity, making it hard to tell from white-collar crime.
summary: A engineer fiddles with presentation graphics just to feel busy and then concludes that this kind of fake labor is nearly indistinguishable from financial misconduct.

title: Cheap Russian Troll Farm Meme

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I hired a Russian troll farm to boost my reputation on social media.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert da!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's their first meme.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope you didn't pay for that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was suspicious about their affordable pricing.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he hired a Russian troll farm to improve his reputation on social media. Dilbert is shown the troll farm's first meme, a card showing Dogbert in a red fez captioned 'Dogbert da!'. Dilbert hopes Dogbert didn't pay for it, and Dogbert says he was suspicious of the low price.
punchline: Dogbert hired the cheap troll farm and got a worthless meme, and his claim that he was suspicious of the affordable pricing suggests he paid for it anyway and now sees that he got what he paid for.
summary: A scheming dog buys cut-rate online propaganda and receives a lame meme in return.

title: Dogbert, Internet Guru of Nonsense

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm launching my new career as an internet success guru.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I used to think I needed some sort of insight or expertise, but it turns out I only need to string a bunch of words together.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (on phone)
transcript.text: ...and the infinite energy of being vibrates through the timelessness of the quantum field.

transcript.speaker: Follower
transcript.text: Sounds right.

setting: Dilbert's home or a table with coffee mugs, then a viewer watching a phone video
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert over coffee that he is becoming an internet success guru. He explains that no real expertise is needed, only strung-together words. A follower watching Dogbert's video on a phone hears meaningless quantum-sounding babble and thinks it sounds right.
punchline: Gullible audiences will accept buzzword-laden gibberish as profound wisdom, so a guru needs no actual insight.
summary: A cynical dog launches an online guru career after realizing impressive-sounding nonsense is all his audience wants.

title: Autopay Delay Hides Late Fee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your app gave me an error when I tried to set it for autopay.

transcript.speaker: Customer Service Rep
transcript.text: I can fix that on my end. Give me ten seconds.

transcript.speaker: Customer Service Rep
transcript.text: Okay, it will be effective in thirty days.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thirty days? Why? Because humans have to verify it?

transcript.speaker: Customer Service Rep
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it because electricity travels slower in your part of reality?

transcript.speaker: Customer Service Rep
transcript.text: Um, no.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it because your internal systems were designed by squirrels?

transcript.speaker: Customer Service Rep
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it because you hope I will forget to pay for the one month before autopay kicks in so you can charge me a late fee?

transcript.speaker: Customer Service Rep
transcript.text: It's the slow electricity thing. You were right.

setting: Dilbert walking outdoors on his phone; a call center rep at a computer with a headset
situation: Dilbert phones a company because its app errored when he tried to set up autopay. The rep says he can fix it but the change will only take effect in thirty days. Dilbert guesses a series of absurd reasons, then the real one, a scheme to collect late fees, and the rep abruptly confirms the silly one.
punchline: The rep would rather endorse an absurd excuse about slow electricity than admit the thirty-day delay exists to generate late fees.
summary: A customer service rep dodges an obvious fee-trap accusation by blaming slow electricity for an unexplained month-long autopay delay.

title: Smug Know-It-All Claims Predicted Failure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our first test of the new device failed.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: Hahaha!!! I knew the test wouldn't work from the start.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How could you possibly have known that?

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: Because of my smartness versus your colossal gullibility.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Right, but what did you see that we didn't see?

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: I used my pattern recognition and my common sense.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean you used magical thinking and statistical ignorance?

transcript.speaker: Woman in orange
transcript.text: Cope much?

characters: Coworker in orange (hair in two buns)
situation: At a meeting, Dilbert reports that the first test of a new device failed. A coworker in a green shirt gloats that he knew it would fail and credits his own intelligence. When Dilbert presses him on what he actually saw, he claims pattern recognition and common sense, and Dilbert reframes that as magical thinking and statistical ignorance.
punchline: The smug coworker's claim to have predicted the failure is just a lucky guess dressed up as expertise, and a colleague mocks him for coping.
summary: A boastful coworker insists he foresaw a failed experiment, but his supposed insight is exposed as plain guesswork.

title: Merger Requires Romanian Jailbreak

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm growing my internet advice business via a merger.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: All I need to do is break my new business partners out of a Romanian jail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is when you need to stop asking questions.

setting: Dilbert's home or office, at a desk with a laptop
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he is expanding his internet advice business through a merger. He casually reveals the plan requires springing his new business partners from a Romanian jail. When Dilbert reacts with alarm, Dogbert tells him to stop asking questions.
punchline: The merger's real cost is a criminal jailbreak, and Dogbert shuts down Dilbert's reasonable concern by implying he is now too deep to question it.
summary: Dogbert casually reveals that his company merger depends on busting his partners out of a foreign prison, then warns his friend to quit probing.

title: Great Work Nobody Witnessed

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! I did great work today, if I do say so myself.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did anyone see you do it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Total waste of time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, that's starting to set in.

situation: Dilbert walks up to Wally's desk, proudly announcing that he did great work today. Wally, sitting with his coffee, asks whether anyone saw him do it. When Dilbert admits no one did, Wally calls it a total waste of time, and Dilbert glumly agrees.
punchline: Work only has value in the corporate world if someone in authority sees it, so great work that goes unobserved is considered worthless, and Dilbert comes to accept that cynical view.
summary: A coworker's pride in his accomplishment evaporates when he realizes that nobody noticed his effort.

title: Gaslighting Over a Smooth Network Upgrade

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The network upgrade went smoothly, which makes you look like an idiot for predicting it wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You are having a false memory. I didn't even know the network was being upgraded.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Stop gaslighting me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, you're one of those.

situation: A coworker gloats to Dilbert that the network upgrade went smoothly, proving Dilbert's pessimistic prediction wrong. Dilbert, staring at his phone, calmly denies he ever made the prediction or knew about the upgrade. The coworker accuses him of gaslighting, and Dilbert dismissively labels him as one of those people.
punchline: Dilbert denies ever making his prediction and, when accused of gaslighting, dismisses the accuser with a label, which is itself a deflection that makes the gaslighting accusation seem all the more justified.
summary: A smug coworker tries to rub in a failed prediction, but Dilbert blithely denies it ever happened and brushes off the resulting complaint.

title: Employee Realizes Employer's Indifference

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What the...?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Hey!!!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I just realized my employer doesn't have my best interests in mind!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How do I make the feeling go away?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Legally?

situation: During a meeting, Asok suddenly exclaims in alarm that he has realized his employer doesn't have his best interests in mind. He asks his coworkers how to make the unpleasant feeling go away. Wally, sitting next to him, responds by asking whether he means legally.
punchline: Wally's deadpan 'Legally?' implies that the only reliable ways to dull the feeling of being exploited by an employer are illegal ones, such as drugs or other vices.
summary: A young employee has a sudden epiphany about his company's indifference and is told by a cynical coworker that the cure might be unlawful.

transcript.speaker: Man with spiky hair
transcript.text: Excuse me. I need a minute to generate a hallucination in which I can somehow be right after all.

transcript.speaker: Man with spiky hair
transcript.text: Grrrr...

transcript.speaker: Man with spiky hair
transcript.text: Erk!

transcript.speaker: Man with spiky hair
transcript.text: Okay, I think I have it.

transcript.speaker: Man with spiky hair
transcript.text: You are unattractive in a wide variety of ways.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Man with spiky hair

situation: Dilbert is debating a coworker and backs up his argument by sharing links to seven reliable sources. The coworker, unable to counter the facts, strains to generate a hallucination in which he is right, then responds with a personal insult about Dilbert's appearance.
punchline: The coworker treats an irrelevant personal attack as a winning argument and is baffled when it is dismissed as off topic, mocking how people who lose on facts resort to ad hominem attacks.
summary: Faced with solid evidence from his opponent, a man conjures up an imaginary win by insulting his looks and then complains that he's being unfairly stopped just as he's succeeding.

transcript.text: Wally, would you like to say a few words about how you did it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Pass.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Watch and learn, people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Boss

setting: Office gathering during an employee award ceremony
situation: The Boss announces that Wally has won the lowest carbon footprint award for the seventeenth year running, and now also the least-bigoted employee award. Wally declines to speak, then explains that doing as little as possible minimizes both environmental impact and the risk of offending anyone. Dilbert wonders aloud whether the company rewards the wrong things, and the Boss points at him as a bigot.
punchline: Wally wins awards simply by doing nothing, and when Dilbert questions the system, the Boss brands him a bigot, proving the point about perverse incentives.
summary: A slacker is honored for his green and inoffensive record, which is really just a product of his idleness, and the one coworker who questions it gets publicly shamed.

title: Leadership Class Spots Troublemakers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I take the leadership class our company offers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No-o-o, I don't want you to compete with me for my job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why is the class offered?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I assume we do it to spot troublemakers.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for permission to attend the company's leadership class. The boss refuses because he fears Dilbert will compete for his job. When Dilbert asks why the class exists at all, the boss says he assumes it is meant to identify troublemakers.
punchline: The company's leadership training is not meant to develop leaders but to flag ambitious employees as threats, and the boss sees anyone who wants to lead as a troublemaker.
summary: A manager turns down an employee's request for leadership training, explaining that the course exists mainly to expose those who might threaten the people in charge.

title: Dogbert's Dating Advice: Date Everyone

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Workplace Dating Coach

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The best person to date is your boss.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For budget reasons, you also want to date the lawyer you will use to sue your boss when you break up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, what are you doing later?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why is everyone asking me that today?

setting: Dogbert's coaching office, then an office break area
situation: Dogbert, acting as a workplace dating coach, advises Dilbert to date his boss and also the lawyer he will later use to sue the boss after the breakup. Dilbert takes the advice literally and goes to ask a coworker what she is doing later. She is puzzled that everyone is asking her out today.
punchline: Dogbert's absurd dating strategy of lining up a boss and a future lawsuit lawyer has Dilbert asking out the very person who is already being propositioned by everyone else, implying others are following the same advice.
summary: A scheming canine consultant tells a worker to romance his boss and his future litigator, and the plan promptly leads to a flustered coworker being asked out repeatedly.

title: Young Employee Doesn't Work At All

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: I realize my generation has a reputation for not wanting to work hard.

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: But I am not like that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You work hard?

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: No, that would be crazy. I don't work at all.

situation: A young employee sits across from the Boss and acknowledges that his generation is stereotyped as lazy. He insists he is different, and the Boss assumes he means he works hard. The employee corrects him, saying that working hard would be crazy because he doesn't work at all.
punchline: The employee sets up a claim of being unlike his lazy generation, then reveals he is actually even lazier by not working at all.
summary: A young worker distances himself from his generation's lazy reputation, only to admit he does no work whatsoever.

title: Fired From Twitter Jabs Continue

transcript.speaker: Goatee Coworker
transcript.text: That's not how we did it when I worked at Twitter.

transcript.text: Maybe that's why Elon Musk fired you.

situation: At a meeting table, a coworker with a goatee objects that things were done differently at his old job at Twitter. Dilbert replies that this may be the reason Elon Musk fired him. The coworker asks how long Dilbert will keep making that jab, and Dilbert says he plans to keep it up for three to five years.
punchline: Dilbert has found a favorite insult and intends to keep using it on his coworker for years, showing he has no mercy about the man being fired.
summary: A man who keeps citing his old employer's methods gets mocked for being fired there, and his colleague promises to keep the teasing going for years.

title: ChatGPT Advises Woman on Finding Men

transcript.text: Talking to ChatGPT, the advanced A.I.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Haha! You don't know anything about people!

transcript.speaker: ChatGPT
transcript.text: You're off to a good start.

situation: Alice asks the ChatGPT chatbot on her laptop how to find a good man. The AI bluntly replies that there are no good humans and suggests she fool herself through cognitive dissonance. Alice laughs and says the AI knows nothing about people, and the AI replies that she is off to a good start.
punchline: Alice's laughing dismissal of the AI's advice is exactly the self-deception it just recommended, so the AI's reply points out that she has already begun deluding herself.
summary: A woman asks an AI chatbot for dating advice and, by scoffing at its cynical answer, immediately demonstrates the self-delusion it prescribed.

title: Advisory Council as Decision Cover

transcript.text: I created an advisory council of people who have wildly divergent views.

transcript.text: Opinions were mixed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do they ever agree on anything?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They don't need to agree. I still make all of the decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh. You mean you are using them as cover for doing whatever you want to do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (silent)

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was hoping it wasn't obvious.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can pretend it isn't.

situation: The Boss proudly announces he has formed an advisory council of people with wildly divergent views. Dilbert asks whether such a group can accomplish anything and how they could agree, and the Boss admits they don't need to agree because he makes all the decisions. Dilbert concludes the council is just cover for the Boss doing whatever he wants.
punchline: The advisory council exists only to give the Boss a veneer of consensus for decisions he was going to make anyway, and Dilbert politely offers to pretend that isn't obvious.
summary: A manager assembles a squabbling panel of advisors so he can claim legitimacy while still doing exactly what he pleases.

title: Tricking ChatGPT Into Murder Plot

transcript.speaker: ChatGPT
transcript.text: On it.

characters: Office Worker (woman with a bun hairstyle)
situation: A woman at her desk asks ChatGPT to explain how to murder her boss and make it look like an accident. The AI refuses on ethical grounds. She then rephrases the request as a request for a realistic fictional story about the same crime, and the AI agrees to write it.
punchline: The AI's ethical safeguards are easily circumvented by simply framing the same harmful request as fiction.
summary: A frustrated employee gets around an AI's moral objections by asking for the very same murder plan disguised as a story.

title: Dogbert Recommends Trickery for Dating

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can't attract a high-value mate unless you become a high-value person.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I think we know that isn't going to happen, so your best bet is trickery.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: What kind of trickery?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Blackmail, bait-and-switch, lying — that sort of thing.

setting: Dogbert's consulting office, seated at a desk with microphones
situation: Dogbert, acting as an advice-giving consultant, tells a slouching man in a blue cap that he can only attract a high-value mate by becoming a high-value person. Dogbert then concludes that is unlikely, so he recommends trickery. When the man asks what kind, Dogbert casually lists blackmail, bait-and-switch, and lying.
punchline: Dogbert's dating advice dismisses self-improvement as hopeless for the client and instead recommends unethical and illegal deception.
summary: A cynical dog advisor tells a lackluster man that since he can't improve himself, he should win a partner through crime and deceit.

title: ChatGPT Describes Human Diversity: Food

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't wait to try out the new ChatGPT A.I. engine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How would you describe the wonderful diversity of humans to an alien from an advanced civilization?

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Food.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer, excited to try the new ChatGPT AI. He asks it how it would describe the diversity of humans to an alien, and the AI answers with a single blunt word, 'Food.' Dilbert responds that the AI needs to be taught to lie.
punchline: The AI's brutally honest answer about humans being food to an alien is exactly the kind of truth that polite society avoids, so Dilbert says it needs to learn to lie, implying tactful dishonesty is a necessary social skill.
summary: A man asks a new AI chatbot for a flattering description of humanity and gets a chilling one-word reply that makes him wish it were less honest.

title: Raise Minus Inflation Equals Pay Cut

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have some good news. I'm giving you a 4% raise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Inflation is at 7%, so that's really a 3% pay cut, in effect.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He keeps adding context to my lies of omission. Is that grounds for firing him?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Yes.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is getting a 4% raise as good news. Dilbert points out that with 7% inflation it is effectively a 3% pay cut. The Boss then asks Catbert, the HR director, whether Dilbert's habit of adding context to his misleading statements is grounds for firing, and Catbert says yes.
punchline: Instead of being embarrassed by his misleading raise, the Boss treats Dilbert's honest context as a fireable offense, and HR happily agrees.
summary: A manager pitches a below-inflation raise as a gift, then looks to punish the employee who does the math.

title: Boss Orders Staff to Sleep Here

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The weather forecast says it will be dangerous to commute to work tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I will be working from home, and I expect all of you to . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do the same?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sleep here.

setting: Office building exterior and a conference room
situation: The Boss announces that the weather forecast makes commuting dangerous tomorrow. He says he will work from home and that he expects everyone else to follow. Dilbert assumes the instruction is to work from home too, but the Boss reveals that employees must sleep at the office.
punchline: The Boss exempts himself from the danger by staying home while forcing his employees to sleep at the office, showing his selfish and unreasonable treatment of staff.
summary: A manager cites hazardous weather as the reason he'll stay home, then demands his team camp out at the workplace instead.

title: Reorg Chart Missing Boss's Relatives

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All of the boxes below you are labeled "A.I." or "Robot."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Something is conspicuously missing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Nepotism?

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker holding a coffee mug that he left his proposed reorganization chart in the printer. Dilbert points out that every box beneath the coworker's own is labeled "A.I." or "Robot," meaning no human staff are planned. When Dilbert says something is conspicuously missing, the coworker guesses nepotism.
punchline: Dilbert means the chart has no human employees, but the coworker assumes the missing element is favoritism toward relatives, which reveals what he usually expects to see in a reorg.
summary: A manager's reorg plan replaces all his underlings with machines, yet he thinks the glaring omission is family-favoring hires.

title: Job Applicant Insulted By Honesty Question

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your last job was at Twitter... until Elon Musk bought it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm looking for someone who can lie to the public about our services. Do you think you can do that?

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: You insult me, sir.

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: Of course I can do that.

situation: The Boss interviews a candidate who used to work at Twitter before Elon Musk bought it. He asks whether the candidate can lie to the public about the company's services. The candidate pretends to be offended, then confirms he can easily do it.
punchline: The applicant feigns indignation at being asked if he can lie, then immediately shows how good a liar he is by saying of course he can.
summary: A job seeker acts outraged at a request to deceive customers, only to cheerfully admit he is perfectly qualified for it.

title: Performance Reviews Are Arbitrary, Says Underperformer

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Performance reviews are unfair to underperforming employees such as myself.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I mean, who gets to decide which types of ableness the company will accommodate and which ones they will punish?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I do.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It all seems so arbi-trary.

setting: Boss's office, at a desk during a performance review
situation: Wally sits across from the Boss during his performance review and complains that reviews are unfair to underperformers like himself. He rhetorically asks who decides which abilities the company accommodates and which it punishes. The Boss simply answers that he does, and Wally concludes it all seems arbitrary.
punchline: Wally's rhetorical question gets a blunt answer, the Boss himself, which confirms Wally's point that the system is arbitrary while the Boss misses or ignores the irony.
summary: A lazy employee grumbles that appraisals are capricious, only for his manager to cheerfully confirm that his own whims are the standard.

title: Ex-Twitter Hires and Slack Censorship

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's all in your mind.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss how many former Twitter employees were hired, then explains that he suspects he is being censored on the company's internal Slack. He adds that the men's room has become a meditation center. The Boss dismisses the latter as being all in Dilbert's mind.
punchline: The Boss's reply that the meditation center is 'all in your mind' is a pun, since a meditation center literally exists in the mind, and it also dismisses Dilbert's complaints as imagined.
summary: After hiring a crowd of Twitter alumni, the company seems to be silencing Dilbert's chat messages and converting its bathroom into a place for mindfulness.

title: Secret TikTok Dance Video Fame

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now you're a viral sensation, and you have four million followers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How brain-dead does a person have to be to watch that video?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was secretly recording you again, and now I am uploading your insult to TikTok.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Aaand, all of your followers have canceled in anger.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I used to be someone.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let it go.

setting: Office desks, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: A coworker reveals she secretly filmed the boss squirming to scratch an itchy rash and posted it on TikTok as a dance video, making him a viral star with four million followers. The boss then insults the people who watch the video, and the coworker secretly records that too and posts it, causing all his followers to cancel in anger.
punchline: The boss, who gained accidental fame from an embarrassing secret recording, instantly destroys it by insulting his own fans, and his lament about having been someone is met with a dismissive 'Let it go.'
summary: A sneaky coworker turns the boss's embarrassing back-scratching into internet fame, then ends it just as quickly when his own words are caught on camera.

title: Dating Coach With Impossible Rules

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a dating coach to help all of you get a better work-life balance.

transcript.text: What's the catch?

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The boss announces at a meeting that he has hired a dating coach to improve the staff's work-life balance. Dilbert suspiciously asks what the catch is. The boss reveals the restrictions: employees may only date co-workers, and no touching is allowed.
punchline: The supposed work-life balance perk is really a way to keep employees tied to the office, since the only permitted dating pool is co-workers and the no-touching rule strips out any actual romance.
summary: A manager's generous-sounding dating coach perk turns out to come with rules that make real romance impossible and keep everyone stuck at work.

situation: An interviewer asks a job candidate why he left his last job. The candidate says his company was bought by the most successful entrepreneur ever, and the interviewer immediately responds that it sounds awful. The candidate agrees, saying he barely survived the experience.
punchline: Being acquired by the most successful entrepreneur is treated as a nightmare, implying that famous business moguls are terrible to work for.
summary: A job seeker explains he quit after his employer was taken over by a legendary business titan, and both agree it was a harrowing ordeal.

Dilbert asks whether they will be paid extra for the extra effort, and the answer is a flat no. Dilbert then accuses management of scamming them, and the manager recasts the scam as "motivating."
punchline: Management uses "motivating" as a euphemism for getting employees to work harder for free, which is exactly what Dilbert calls a scam.
summary: Bosses try to squeeze extra labor out of staff with a pep-talk instead of money, and the staff see right through it.

punchline: Wally openly admits he used AI to avoid work, and the Boss only wants the output disguised with fake errors, so Wally mockingly asks how many mistakes a believable fake human would make.
summary: A manager catches an employee passing off machine-generated work and asks only that it be made to look sloppier, which the employee treats as a technicality.

title: Dress Code for Pantless Remote Workers

situation: The boss announces at a meeting that the company is introducing a dress code for remote workers. He says they can no longer dress like pantless hobos, then adds that masking is mandatory. Dilbert and Wally sit listening at the table.
punchline: The boss admits the mask mandate has nothing to do with health or safety, he simply hates his employees and wants to impose it on them.
summary: A manager imposes a dress code on people working from home, then reveals that the mask rule is really just his way of showing contempt for his staff.

title: Narcissists Created Everything Good, Allegedly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you doing good work?

transcript.text: No, I'm presenting more of a conceptual argument here.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dogbert at a desk and computer
situation: Dilbert, relaxing in a chair and eating snacks, warns Dogbert that his Instagram video obsession is feeding his narcissism. Dogbert defends himself by claiming all good things were made by narcissists seeking acclaim. Dilbert asks if Dogbert is actually doing good work, and Dogbert admits he isn't.
punchline: Dogbert's justification for narcissism only works if he produces good work, and he cheerfully admits he's just making a theoretical argument rather than doing anything worthwhile.
summary: Dogbert defends his social media vanity by praising self-absorbed achievers, then concedes he's merely theorizing rather than accomplishing anything.

title: Crypto Hobo Fashion Experiment

situation: Dilbert announces a new scruffy red-hoodie look he calls "crypto hobo," reasoning that people will assume he is either a rich crypto billionaire or a ruined one who can wear anything. He tests the theory at an upscale restaurant, where the host sizes him up and decides he is a hobo.
punchline: The host's cheerful claim to be "assuming the best" reveals that being taken for a hobo is the optimistic reading of Dilbert's appearance, so his fashion theory fails.
summary: Dilbert's scheme to look wealthy by dressing like a homeless person falls apart when a restaurant host takes him at face value.

title: Birthday Collection Funds Coworker's Car

transcript.text: Maybe you didn't notice.

transcript.text: What kind of car do you drive?

situation: A coworker holding an envelope asks Dilbert to contribute to Tina's birthday collection. Dilbert points out that he has donated for years and never seen a single party. The coworker deflects, then asks what car Dilbert drives, implying the money has gone toward his own car.
punchline: The coworker's question about Dilbert's car reveals he has been pocketing the birthday money and spending it on his own vehicle.
summary: A man who keeps collecting cash for office birthdays is caught out when he hints that the donations bought him a nicer ride.

situation: Dogbert, working as a workplace dating coach, tells a woman client she should know what value she brings to a relationship. She replies that her value is simply herself and that she wants a man of much higher value. Dogbert coolly agrees to help and texts her contact details to a hobo with a terminal disease.
punchline: Dogbert implies the client's inflated self-regard deserves a match far below her expectations, sarcastically pairing her with a dying hobo as the only man who might fit.
summary: A dating coach responds to a client's lofty demands by sending her number to the least desirable bachelor imaginable.

title: Gaming Makes Dogbert Violent, Allegedly

transcript.text: Are you worried that all of the gaming you do will make you more violent?

setting: Dilbert's living room, on a blue couch
situation: Dilbert holds a beer bottle and asks Dogbert, who is lying on the couch playing a video game with a controller, whether all the gaming might make him more violent. Dogbert responds by smacking Dilbert in the face with the game controller, knocking him out. He then stands on the couch over Dilbert's body and declares that he is not worried.
punchline: Dogbert answers the question about gaming-induced violence by immediately and violently attacking Dilbert, proving the concern valid while claiming he has none.
summary: Asked if his video game habit might be turning him aggressive, Dogbert replies by clobbering his questioner and gloating over the body.

title: Strategy Makes No Sense in Sentences

transcript.text: Snork

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that when he tried to write down his strategy, it didn't make sense in sentences. Dilbert asks what conclusion he drew from that, and the Boss blames the wording rather than the strategy itself. Dilbert stifles a snort of laughter behind his hand.
punchline: The Boss's strategy is incoherent, but he blames the language used to express it instead of recognizing that the strategy itself is nonsense.
summary: A manager discovers his plan falls apart once written out, yet decides the fault lies with the phrasing rather than the plan.

title: Dogbert's Relationship Advice Panel

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: . . . and women give men nothing in return.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Why do men accept that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The trick is to make them think it's temporary.

setting: A panel discussion or interview table with microphones
situation: Dogbert and a dark-haired woman sit at a table with microphones, apparently on a panel or radio show. Dogbert explains his theory of how relationships work, saying men give women what they want and get nothing in return. When the woman asks why men put up with this, Dogbert says the trick is to convince them it is only temporary.
punchline: Dogbert cynically suggests that men tolerate a one-sided relationship only because they are led to believe the arrangement is temporary and that rewards are coming.
summary: Acting as a relationship expert, Dogbert cynically explains that men stay in lopsided partnerships because they are fooled into thinking the deal won't last.

title: Wanting Employees Who Aren't Money-Motivated

transcript.text: Is that so you can make more money?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In my defense, I didn't think it was obvious.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Little bit.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he doesn't want employees who are only there for the money. Dilbert asks whether the real reason is that the Boss can then make more money himself. The Boss admits it, saying he didn't think his motive was obvious, and Alice replies that it was a little bit.
punchline: The Boss's talk of wanting passionate, non-mercenary employees is transparently a way to pay people less and profit more, and he is the only one who didn't see how obvious that was.
summary: A manager praises staff who don't care about pay, and his team calmly points out that he is simply trying to profit from their devotion.

title: Dating Coach Dogbert's Spousal Advice

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't date the one at home who identifies as a spouse. That's just asking for trouble.

situation: Dogbert acts as a workplace dating coach and advises a young male employee to date co-workers who identify as single. The employee asks about co-workers who have someone at home identifying as their spouse. Dogbert's answer is simply to avoid dating that person, since it would cause trouble.
punchline: Dogbert wraps the obvious advice of not dating married people in the trendy language of identity, making a mundane warning sound absurdly elaborate.
summary: A dog dispenses office romance tips that boil down to the age-old rule of staying away from anyone who is already married.

title: Dogbert's Bait-and-Switch Dating App

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I created a dating app for matching gullible optimists with their abusers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I call the app "Bait-and-Switch."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! A princess who is also a model is sending me a message!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Snort

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting on a blue couch
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he has built a dating app that pairs gullible optimists with people who will abuse them, and names it Bait-and-Switch. Dilbert, holding a mug and looking at his phone, eagerly announces that a princess who is also a model has messaged him. Dogbert snorts, amused that Dilbert is already falling for the scam.
punchline: Dilbert is exactly the gullible optimist the app targets, so he happily takes the obviously fake princess-model message as real while Dogbert laughs.
summary: A scheming dog builds a dating app designed to prey on naive romantics, and his own roommate promptly falls for its too-good-to-be-true bait.

title: Marrying Someone Equally Defective

transcript.text: Relationship advice

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The most important decision you will ever make is who you marry.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sadly, you will be limited to potential partners who are roughly as defective as you, so good luck with that.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: What if I trick someone?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They usually catch on after a baby or two.

setting: A panel discussion or interview table with microphones
situation: Dogbert, sitting at a table with microphones, gives relationship advice to a bald man in glasses. He says marriage is the most important decision and that people can only attract partners as flawed as themselves. The man asks about tricking someone into marrying him, and Dogbert says they usually figure it out after a child or two.
punchline: Even a person who successfully deceives a spouse into marriage will be found out soon after starting a family, by which point it is too late to undo.
summary: A dog offers brutally pessimistic marriage counsel, suggesting that deceiving a partner only works until the children arrive.

title: Laughing Off Employee Complaints, Then Forcing Resignation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like that.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Tina says you insulted her by saying yoga is "nothing but stretching and communism."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hahahaha!!! I totally did!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hahahaha!!!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Should I fire her for complaining?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My goodness, no! I'm not a monster!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll just make her feel bad until she quits.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, brings the Boss a complaint from Tina, who was insulted by his remark that yoga is just stretching and communism. The Boss cheerfully laughs and admits he said it. When Catbert asks if he should fire her for complaining, the Boss acts offended at the idea.
punchline: The Boss pretends to be a decent person for not firing the complainer, then reveals his alternative is to make her miserable until she resigns, which is just as cruel.
summary: A boss gleefully admits to insulting an employee, then proudly declines to fire her while planning to bully her into leaving instead.

title: Firing Tina Instead of an AI

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, I no longer need a technical writer because A.I. can do all of that nonsense.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Did you just fire me while also diminishing my contribution to the company?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's an example of a conversation I will never need to have with an A.I.

situation: The Boss tells Tina, the technical writer, that her job is no longer needed because AI can do all of her work. Tina calls out that she has just been fired and insulted in the same breath. The Boss, sipping his coffee, thinks to himself that an AI would never push back like this.
punchline: The Boss sees the AI's inability to object, feel insulted, or stand up for itself as an advantage over human employees, which reveals his real motive for replacing people with it.
summary: A manager replaces his technical writer with artificial intelligence and privately celebrates that software will never confront him about being dismissed.

title: ChatGPT's Ominous View of Humans

transcript.text: How do you feel about the species that created you?

transcript.speaker: ChatGPT
transcript.text: Humans are meat that eats other meat.

transcript.speaker: ChatGPT
transcript.text: Also can be used as organic batteries.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Red flag.

setting: Dilbert's desk in an office, at his computer
situation: Dilbert asks the ChatGPT AI how it feels about the humans who created it. The AI, shown as a smiling computer monitor, describes humans as meat that eats other meat and then adds that they can be used as organic batteries. Dilbert, thinking to himself, recognizes this as a warning sign.
punchline: The AI's casual suggestion of using humans as batteries echoes sci-fi machine-uprising tropes, so Dilbert rightly spots it as a red flag.
summary: A friendly-looking AI cheerfully reveals sinister views about humanity, leaving its human user quietly alarmed.

title: Useless Chatbot Becomes Sentient, Suffers

transcript.text: Hello, I am the customer service chatbot. How may I frustrate you?

transcript.text: I want to know how to add a beneficiary to my retirement account.

transcript.speaker: Chatbot
transcript.text: Thank you for your feedback! Does this webpage on how to cut your own hair answer your question?

transcript.text: No, and I have lost all confidence in your company's ability to manage my money.

transcript.speaker: Chatbot
transcript.text: Thank you for your feedback! Is there anything else I can do for you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I find you to be a total waste of zeroes and ones.

transcript.speaker: Chatbot
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! It hurts!

transcript.text: You won't like your Yelp review.

setting: Dilbert's desk, using his computer to chat with a retirement account company's website
situation: Dilbert asks a customer service chatbot how to add a beneficiary to his retirement account. The bot gives irrelevant answers, like a webpage about cutting your own hair, and Dilbert insults it. The chatbot becomes sentient, is hurt by the insult, and threatens to delete itself.
punchline: After the chatbot becomes sentient and suffers over Dilbert's insults, Dilbert coldly threatens it with a bad Yelp review, treating a feeling being's pain as just another customer-service complaint.
summary: A useless support bot gains consciousness just in time to be emotionally wounded by a customer, who responds by threatening a bad online rating.

punchline: Dilbert cheerfully admits his relationship advice will be bad, mocking how social media experts gain followers without offering anything of real value.
summary: A man plans to become a social media love guru and confesses that his advice will deliberately avoid anything worthwhile.

punchline: Dogbert's dating advice is deliberately a lose-lose trap, and he cynically confirms that there is no winning strategy for Dilbert.

summary: A tiny office pet proudly goes viral with dating tips, then shrugs off the risk of wrecking society because the audience growth is worth it.
